teaser.en: Its scent is famous in perfume; at the coast its flowers are worn on clothes and in hair, and scattered on beds.

summary.en: Mlangilangi is the ylang-ylang tree, an introduced perfume tree whose fragrant, drooping yellow flowers Digo people use as decoration. Its Digo name comes from the English name.

about.en:
*Mlangilangi* is a fast-growing tree with drooping branches and large, glossy, pointed leaves. Its flowers hang in clusters and have six long, narrow, twisted petals that start green and turn yellow as they ripen, when they give off a strong, sweet scent. The fruits are clusters of small dark berries.

Pakia counts it among the plants that Digo speakers can identify from their flowers, because the flowers are valued as perfume.

where.en: It is native to South-East Asia and was brought to the Kenya coast for cultivation. Pakia, following Beentje, says it has since gone wild there. Look for it in gardens and around homes.

uses.en: The flowers are best known worldwide as the source of ylang-ylang oil for perfume. On the Digo coast, the flowers are made into rosettes and worn on clothes and in the hair, or placed on beds, for their beauty and scent.

culture.en: Pakia describes how flowers are used for beauty and romance among the Digo. Rosettes of *mlangilangi*, *chiluwa* (*Mkilua fragrans*) and jasmine are worn or laid on beds. Together with henna patterns and flower-pattern fabrics, these beautifications are called *maruwa*, from *ruwa*, a word for beauty.

names.en: Pakia gives *mlangilangi* as one of three Digo plant names that agree with scientific or Western names. It was adopted from the English *ylang-ylang* when the tree was introduced. No Swahili name is given in the sources.

reason.en: Mkilua, the other perfume flower worn as maruwa
Henna, also part of maruwa beautification
Wild jasmine, relative of the jasmine worn with it
